claims.text: A machine-learning-driven optimization of thermo-mechanical processing can concurrently improve strength and ductility in metallic alloys.
Optimized thermo-mechanical processing can generate a multiphase microstructure with tailored coherent precipitates.
Traditional strengthening routes typically increase strength at the expense of ductility.
Alloys produced by traditional strengthening routes may have coarse grains or single-mode precipitation.
A machine-learning model can analyze experimental and simulation datasets to design optimized heat-treatment and deformation protocols.
The proposed concurrent improvement applies under room-temperature mechanical loading.
Refractory alloys can form dual or multiphase structures during thermo-mechanical processing.
High-entropy alloys can form the controllable dual or multiphase structures required by the proposed method.
The desired structural mediator is a multiphase microstructure containing coherent fine lamellae and nanoscale precipitates.
Coherent precipitates impede dislocation motion while permitting continuous plastic deformation.
A machine-learning model can identify the precise processing parameters controlling precipitate evolution, size, and distribution.
Heavy cold rolling increases dislocation density and creates dislocation walls that provide a structural basis for subsequent controllable precipitation.
Tailored precipitates increase strength by hindering dislocation motion.
The tailored multiphase microstructure maintains or promotes plasticity pathways that retain ductility.
Machine-learning-optimized thermo-mechanical processing will produce a significantly better strength–ductility combination than conventional processing.
The method should be most effective in alloy systems where multiphase or complex precipitation microstructures can form and be controlled.
The method may be less effective in alloy systems inherently prone to brittleness.
The method may be less effective when phase stability is not maintained under operating conditions.
Preliminary studies support qualitative strength–ductility improvements from the proposed machine-learning approach.
The quantitative gains remain uncertain and require experimental validation.
